chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 121 to 128, the neythal decade spoken to the lord of the shore: by our reading the friend answering a husband who denies another woman, each poem opening 'did we not see your woman?' and showing her as a child at sea play, asking a heron for a lost jewel, filling the sea with sand to avenge a stolen doll, weeping red-eyed for it, and feeding a doll from a breast that has no milk.

121.reading: The friend asks the lord of the shore whether they did not see his woman, the one who leapt into the clear-waved sea and stood there with her sea-holly garland soaking.
121.nuance: The opening question is a rebuttal: கண்டிகும் அல்லமோ presumes he has denied her, and the friend proves the woman exists by describing her at play, so the evidence and the insult are the same picture.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea-holly of the backwater and the open sea

122.reading: Did we not see his woman, the friend says, who, when her bright jewel fell on the high sand, went asking the white heron about it?
122.nuance: Asking a heron after a lost jewel is the act of a child who thinks birds answer; the friend uses it to measure the rival's simplicity. The verb is read as வினவுவோள் (she who asks); the line's வினைவு does not give a sense as written.

123.reading: Did we not see his woman, says the friend, leaping into the waves of the cool great sea while her bright-browed playmates shouted?
123.nuance: ஆயம், the troop of girl companions, belongs to an unmarried girl's world; placing the rival inside it says she is not yet a woman at all.

124.reading: Did we not see his woman, the friend says, who, because the wave took her sand doll, scoops up fine sand to fill in the sea?
124.nuance: The wave's theft is implied, not stated (வெளவலின் has no subject in the line); 125 names it, தெண்டிரை. Filling the sea with sand to punish it is the folly the friend wants the husband to see in his choice.

125.reading: Did we not see his woman, the friend says, who stood weeping till her kohl-lined eyes went red because the clear wave seized her doll?
125.nuance: The red eyes from weeping are the sign the akam poems give a deserted wife; here they come from a lost toy, which turns the heroine's grief into a child's tantrum in the rival.

126.reading: Did we not see his woman, says the friend, who plunges into the great wave of the clear sea while swarms of bees crowd about her kohl eyes?
126.nuance: Bees swarming to the eyes treat them as flowers, the one praise in the decade; even this is play, the girl ducking under the wave to escape them.

127.reading: Did we not see his woman, the friend says, who wears a thumbai garland slung across her chest, its fine ornaments over breasts only just budding?
127.nuance: The sense turns on விலங்குவோள், read here as wearing the garland crosswise; it could also be she who turns aside or bars the way with her chest. இளமுலை, a young breast, keeps the decade's point: the rival is barely grown.

128.reading: Did we not see his woman, says the friend, feeding a doll that cannot eat from her empty breast that no child has sucked and that has no milk?
128.nuance: The decade's sharpest barb closes it: the girl playing mother with a dry breast is set against the wife who has borne his children, so the husband's rival is, in the friend's telling, still rehearsing the life the wife already lives.

links.note: Both answer a husband who denies the other woman with the same verb, கண்டிகும் (we saw): Natrinai 20's heroine describes a woman leaving his bed with crushed garland and loosened hair, Ainkurunuru 121's friend a girl leaping into the sea with her garland soaked.
links.teaches: The one retort to a denial can be built two opposite ways, by showing the rival as a spent lover whose body carries his marks or as a child at play, so the 'we saw her' formula's sting lies in how the witness chooses to portray the woman, not in the seeing.

links.note: In Natrinai 30 the friend tells the denying husband கண்டனென் ... கண்டு எவன்செய்கோ, I saw, and what can I do having seen; in Ainkurunuru 122 the friend's having seen becomes a mocking portrait of a girl asking a heron for her jewel.
links.teaches: Natrinai 30 admits that the friend's witness gives her no power over the husband, and the Ainkurunuru decade shows what she does with that powerless witness instead: she turns it into ridicule, the one weapon left to a go-between who cannot compel.

links.note: Purananuru 243's old man remembers garlanding a doll of packed sand and leaping into deep water as the untaught youth he has lost; Ainkurunuru 124 shows a girl with a sand doll punishing the sea that took it.
links.teaches: The same shore games of sand dolls and leaps into water are, in the puram elegy, the innocence age mourns, and in the akam barb, the proof that a man has taken up with a child, so the scene of youth carries nostalgia or contempt according to who recalls it and for what end.

links.note: Both have the wife's side describe the rival by her dress: in Natrinai 170 the girl in a leaf skirt who comes alone to the festival is a danger the wives must rise against, while in Ainkurunuru 127 the garland across budding breasts marks her as a child of no account.
links.teaches: On a defensible reading the two friends make incompatible claims about what a young rival's youth means, a strength that may overwhelm the household or a weakness that makes her laughable, showing that the wife's party had no settled verdict on the young courtesan and chose the one their moment needed.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; the speaker (the friend, to the husband) is inferred from the decade title and the refrain, and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
Only eight poems (121 to 128) of the decade survive in our text; 129 and 130 are absent.
122 line 1 reads கண்டகும் where every other poem of the decade has the refrain கண்டிகும்; likely a misprint.
122 line 3 வினைவு வோளே gives no clear sense; read as வினவுவோளே (she who asks), uncertain.
125 line 1 lacks the refrain's last word கேளே, present in every other poem of the decade.
126 line 2 begins யுண்கண், carrying the glide from the refrain's கேளே across the line break; the word is உண்கண்.
127 line 3 விலங்கு வோளே is divided; the sense of விலங்குவோள் is uncertain.
